what_its_for: Prednisone is a corticosteroid (steroid) medicine used to reduce swelling, redness, and irritation in your body. It treats many conditions including allergic reactions, asthma, arthritis, skin problems, lupus, certain blood disorders, and other inflammatory conditions. It works by calming down your immune system when it is overreacting.
how_to_take: Take prednisone by mouth exactly as your doctor tells you. Always take it with food or milk to help prevent stomach upset. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water. If you are taking it once a day, try to take it in the morning with breakfast, as this matches your body's natural hormone cycle and may help you sleep better at night. Do not suddenly stop taking prednisone without talking to your doctor first, especially if you have been taking it for more than a few weeks — your doctor will slowly lower your dose over time.
dosing: Your dose depends on your specific condition, weight, and how your body responds. Doses can range from as low as 5 mg to 60 mg or more per day. Your doctor may start you on a higher dose and then slowly lower it as you improve. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and do not change your dose on your own. If you are taking it every other day, take it only on the days your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. If you miss a dose and are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store prednisone at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication past its expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid contact with people who are sick or have infections such as chickenpox, measles, or the flu, because prednisone weakens your immune system and makes it harder to fight off infections. Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the nasal flu spray or shingles vaccine) while taking prednisone without checking with your doctor first. Limit alcohol use, as it can increase the risk of stomach bleeding and other side effects. Avoid taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen without your doctor's approval, as this increases your risk of stomach ulcers. Try to avoid eating large amounts of salty foods, as prednisone can cause you to retain water and raise your blood pressure.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: signs of serious infection such as fever, chills, or a cough that does not go away; severe stomach pain or blood in your stool; sudden vision changes; severe mood swings, depression, or thoughts of hurting yourself; muscle weakness; unusual weight gain or swelling in your legs or ankles; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurred vision; chest pain or difficulty breathing; or any signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, or swelling of the face or throat. Also call your doctor if you accidentally stop taking prednisone suddenly and feel unusually tired, dizzy, or weak.
when_it_works: How quickly prednisone works depends on your condition. For allergic reactions or acute flare-ups, you may feel better within a few hours to a day or two. For chronic conditions like arthritis or inflammatory diseases, it may take several days to notice a significant improvement. Keep taking it as prescribed even if you feel better, and do not stop without your doctor's approval.
special_populations: Children: Prednisone can slow growth in children when used long-term. Your child's doctor will use the lowest effective dose and monitor growth carefully. Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Talk to your doctor before taking prednisone. It may be used during pregnancy when the benefits outweigh the risks, but it can pass into breast milk. Older adults: Older adults may have a higher risk of bone loss (osteoporosis), high blood pressure, and blood sugar problems. Your doctor may recommend calcium, vitamin D, or bone-protecting medicines. People with diabetes: Prednisone can raise your blood sugar levels, so you may need to monitor your blood sugar more closely and your diabetes medicine doses may need to be adjusted. People with liver disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have liver problems. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all your medical conditions and medicines before starting prednisone.
